response: Koine Greek is the common dialect of Greek that was spoken and written during the Hellenistic and Roman periods, roughly from the 4th century BCE to the 4th century CE. It was based primarily on the Attic dialect but included elements from other Greek dialects. Koine served as the lingua franca across the Mediterranean world and the Near East under Greek and later Roman rule. It is also the language of the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible) and the New Testament of the Christian Bible.

In the context of ancient Greek, Attic refers to the dialect of Greek spoken in Athens and the surrounding region of Attica during the Classical period (5th-4th centuries BCE). It was the most prestigious and influential Greek dialect, forming the basis for Koine Greek and having significant literary and cultural importance. The works of Classical Greek authors like Plato, Thucydides, and the Attic orators were written in this dialect, which is known for its refined and sophisticated style.

Doric was one of the major dialects of ancient Greek, primarily spoken in the Peloponnese, Crete, and some Aegean islands. It was characterized by distinctive linguistic features, such as preserving the ancient Greek sound system more conservatively than other dialects. Doric was the language of Sparta and was used in Dorian Greek colonies. In literature, it was notably used in choral poetry, particularly in the works of poets like Pindar, and in some regional inscriptions and local literature.

Ionic was another major dialect of ancient Greek, primarily spoken in Ionia (the western coast of Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey) and some Aegean islands like Chios and Samos. It was closely related to Attic Greek and formed the basis of the Attic-Ionic dialect group. Ionic was the language of early Greek prose writers like Herodotus and was used in epic poetry, most famously in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey. It was known for its distinctive linguistic features and was influential in the development of Koine Greek.
